title: A Nuclear Reactor Still Glows After You Switch It Off
hook: Shut a reactor down and the fission stops — but the fuel keeps emitting antineutrinos for months. Physicists have now caught that ghostly afterglow for the first time.
key_points: Fission fragments left in the fuel are radioactive and keep beta-decaying long after the chain reaction ends, each decay releasing an antineutrino.
Researchers detected this residual antineutrino signal from a shut-down reactor for the first time.
The measured glow closely matched predictions from the known decay chains in the core and in nearby spent-fuel pools.
Antineutrinos pass straight through shielding, so they report on the fuel's true state from outside the building.
That makes the technique attractive for safeguards: verifying what is in a reactor even when it is offline.
content_html: A reactor's power does not fall to zero the moment the control rods drop. The chain reaction stops, but the fuel is now full of fission fragments — unstable nuclei that keep beta-decaying for months. Every one of those decays throws off an antineutrino, and physicists have now detected that residual glow for the first time.
extra_html:
The measured signal matched predictions built from the known decay chains inside the core and in the spent-fuel pools next door, which is the encouraging part: the model of what is sitting in the fuel can be checked against a real measurement. Because antineutrinos pass through shielding, containment, and rock essentially unimpeded, a detector outside the building sees the fuel's true state without needing access to it.

That is the practical hook. Antineutrino detectors have long been floated as a non-intrusive safeguards tool for verifying reactor activity; being able to read the signal from a reactor that is offline extends the idea to the periods when monitoring is hardest. See ScienceDaily's report for details on the detection.

related.title: Neutrinos From Inside the Earth Are Mapping the Mantle
related.hook: You can't drill to the mantle, but its radioactive decays leak neutrinos straight through the planet — and detectors are starting to read them.

related.title: Catching the Ghost Particle
related.hook: Trillions of neutrinos stream through your body every second, yet they almost never touch anything. To catch even a few, physicists build some of the most audacious detectors ever conceived.

related.title: Nuclear Fission
related.hook: Split one heavy nucleus and it releases neutrons that split more — a chain reaction that, tamed, lights cities, and unleashed, levels them.

related.title: Radioactivity and Half-Life
related.hook: You can't predict when a single unstable atom will decay, yet a huge sample decays on a clock so precise we use it to date rocks billions of years old.

flashcards.prompt: Why does a reactor keep emitting antineutrinos after it is shut down?
flashcards.back_html: The fission fragments left in the fuel are themselves radioactive. They keep beta-decaying for months, and every beta decay emits an antineutrino — long after the chain reaction has stopped.

flashcards.prompt: What property makes antineutrinos useful for monitoring a reactor from outside?

choices.text: They barely interact, so they pass through shielding and containment unimpeded
They are absorbed by concrete, so the wall thickness reveals the core's power
They travel faster than light, so the signal arrives before the fission event

flashcards.explanation_html: Antineutrinos are famously reluctant to interact. Nothing practical stops them, so the signal leaving the core reports on the fuel's actual state regardless of how well the reactor is shielded.
